lead: Abraham stands at the center of both readings. In Genesis, God gives him a new name and an everlasting covenant. In John, Jesus claims that Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and then says the words that bring stones into people’s hands: “before Abraham was, I am.” The covenant with Abraham leads to the one Abraham longed to see. The key words are covenant, name and I am.

set: Abram is ninety-nine years old (17:1), and he and Sarai have no son together. God has made him promises (Genesis 12; 15), and he now confirms them with a covenant and a new name, under the title “God Almighty”. The chapter goes on to give circumcision as the sign of the covenant and to promise Isaac (17:10–21).
str: v. 3: Abram falls on his face.
vv. 4–6: “As for me”: God’s side: many nations, a new name, kings.
vv. 7–8: the everlasting covenant and the land.
v. 9: “As for you”: Abraham’s side: keep the covenant.
kw: A solemn bond that makes two parties belong to one another. The word comes over and over in this chapter. God is the one who starts it and who holds it in being.
ancestor of a multitude of nations
The new name Abraham sounds like these words. Abram means something like “exalted father”, and for an old man with no son by Sarai, each use of the new name was a promise not yet seen.
‘Ôlām points to a long, unbounded time. God does not take back what he has given here.
vv: As for me, this is my covenant with you: You shall be the ancestor of a multitude of nations.
God speaks first, and he speaks of what he will do. The obligation (v. 9) comes after the gift.
No longer shall your name be Abram, but your name shall be Abraham;
In the Bible a new name means a new calling (compare Genesis 32:28; Matthew 16:18). Abraham is named for what he cannot yet see.
to be God to you and to your offspring after you.
This is the heart of every covenant in Scripture: “I will be your God”. Everything else, even the land, serves this.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God called Abraham to gather together scattered humanity, and made his descendants the trustees of the promise (CCC 59–60). The Jewish people remain the first to hear the word of God, to whom the covenant belongs, “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4). In the Roman Canon the Church calls Abraham “our father in faith”.

set: This is the close of the long dispute in the Temple at the festival of Booths. The argument has been about Abraham, and it now reaches its peak. As before, “the Jews” in this Gospel refers to those of his hearers who are in dispute with him, not to a whole people. To them, Jesus’ words sounded like blasphemy, and they respond as they believe the law requires (Leviticus 24:16).
str: v. 51: keep my word and never see death.
vv. 52–53: “Abraham died.” “Who do you claim to be?”
vv. 57–59: “before Abraham was, I am”; the stones.
kw: A word for exultant joy, used often in the Greek psalms. Some Jewish writings speak of God showing Abraham the ages to come. John says that what Abraham longed for was this day.
The contrast is in the verbs. Genesthai means “to come to be”, and Abraham did. Eimi simply means “I am”. Jesus does not say “I was”.
vv: Very truly, I tell you, whoever keeps my word will never see death.
They think he means the end of bodily life, and so they point to Abraham’s grave. He means the life that death cannot end (compare 11:25–26).
Your ancestor Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.
Jesus does not set Abraham aside. He calls him their ancestor and makes him a witness to his coming.
Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.

Here the “I am” of this chapter is plain. St Augustine says that Jesus does not say “I was” because the words belong to the Godhead, for whom there is no past or future (in substance). The Catechism lists this saying among those that only his divine identity can justify (CCC 590).
So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
His hour has not yet come (compare 8:20). He goes out of the Temple. When the hour does come, he will lay down his life of his own accord (10:18).
ch: The Church’s faith in the Son, “God from God, Light from Light”, rests on sayings like this one. The Catechism also explains that such a claim was a real stumbling block for many in Israel, and it treats those who rejected him with care (CCC 589–591). The Passion is not to be charged against the Jewish people (CCC 597).

study: God gave Abram a new name before he had a son. What new thing has God begun in me that I cannot yet see?
Who do I say Jesus is when I pray? Does “I am” change how I bring him my fear of death?
